opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question, and I think the word "trustworthy" is doing a lot of work there. For me, trust doesn't come from a model saying the right things. It comes from the model actually understanding the world it's talking about.

Right now, a lot of what we call intelligence is built mostly on language. Language is incredibly powerful, but it's a compressed, secondhand description of reality. A model can be very fluent and still not really know how the physical world works: how objects persist, how things move, what causes what. When there's a gap between fluency and understanding, you get hallucinations, overconfidence, behavior that looks smart until it suddenly isn't. That's where trust breaks down.

So one part of my answer, which is my own research bias, is grounding. If we want AI to be a real intelligent entity and not just a very good autocomplete, it needs to perceive and model the world more directly, through vision, through interaction, through something like a world model. Humans trust each other partly because we share the same physical reality and roughly the same intuitions about it. An AI that shares that grounding is easier to predict, and predictability is a big part of trust.

The second part is honesty about uncertainty. A trustworthy system should know what it doesn't know and be willing to say so. Today we often optimize models to always produce an answer that sounds good, and that works against trust.

The third part is less technical. It's about openness and the research community. I care a lot about open science. If only a few closed labs understand how these systems are built and evaluated, it's very hard for society to trust them, no matter how good they are. Trust needs to be earned in public: shared benchmarks, reproducible results, people being able to poke at the system and find its failures.

And finally, I'd say we should be humble. We're still very early. Calling AI a "new intelligent entity" is exciting, but we shouldn't rush to trust it the way we'd trust a person. Trust should grow step by step as the systems show that their understanding is real, not just apparent. Our job as researchers is to close that gap between looking intelligent and actually being intelligent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why shared physical grounding can support trust, but it does not ask why people trust their children and other people while fearing AI.

r002.rationale: It presents grounding through direct perception and interaction, including world models, as a way to make AI’s understanding more real and its behavior more predictable and trustworthy.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question, and I think it's actually the right question, because for a long time our field was mostly obsessed with capability—can the model do the task, what's the benchmark number—and trustworthiness was treated as something you bolt on afterwards. I've come to think that's backwards.

Let me start from where I actually work, which is vision and representation learning. When I look at a lot of the current multimodal systems, there's a strange situation: the language side is very strong, but the visual side is often surprisingly fragile. We did some work on this—we literally constructed pairs of images that look nearly identical to the model's encoder but are clearly different to any human, and the models would confidently give the same answer for both. That's a small example, but it gets at what I mean by trustworthiness. A system that is confidently wrong about something a child can see is not a system you can trust, no matter how eloquent it is. Fluency is not understanding. So part one, for me, is that trust has to be grounded. The model's internal representation of the world has to actually track the world. If the perception is shallow, everything built on top of it is shallow, and no amount of alignment training on the output fixes that.

Part two is about honesty regarding uncertainty. Humans trust other humans not because they're always right, but because we have some sense of when they know and when they're guessing. Current models are very bad at this. They're trained in a way that rewards producing an answer, so they produce one. I think a trustworthy intelligent entity has to be able to say "I'm not sure," or "I can't see that clearly," and have that statement actually correlate with reality. That's partly a training-objective problem and partly an architecture problem, and honestly we don't have a clean solution yet.

Part three—and this is maybe the more philosophical one—is that I don't think trust is a property of the model alone. It's a property of the relationship between the model and the people using it, and that relationship is built on things like transparency, reproducibility, and openness. This is why I care so much about open research. If the only entities that understand how these systems work are a handful of companies, then "trust" just means "trust us," and that's not trust, that's faith. When the community can inspect the data, the training recipe, the failure modes, then trust becomes something you can verify rather than something you're asked to accept. I've always tried to do my research in a way where the recipe is simple enough that others can reproduce and interrogate it, and I think that ethic matters even more now.

And there's a fourth thing I'd add, which is humility about what we're building. We throw around words like "intelligent entity," and I'm not sure we fully understand what we mean. These systems learn from human data, so they inherit our strengths and our biases. Treating them as trustworthy by default would be a mistake; treating them as hopeless would also be a mistake. The honest position is that we're in the middle of figuring it out, and the way to make progress is to keep testing them against the real world—with vision, with interaction, with embodiment eventually—rather than only against text that we ourselves wrote.

So if I had to compress it: ground the perception, calibrate the confidence, keep the process open, and stay honest about how early we are. Trust is earned through those things, not declared.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses trust and says people trust others partly because they can tell when they are guessing, but it does not ask why people trust children and other people while fearing AI.

r002.rationale: The candidate says trustworthy AI needs an internal representation that tracks the world, presenting grounded perception as a requirement for trustworthiness.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do we mean by trustworthy? A system can be very capable and still be unreliable. It can give you a convincing answer, but that doesn’t mean it understands where its answer stops being valid.

For me, trust has to come from evidence. We need to understand when these systems work, when they fail, and whether they can communicate uncertainty. And we need to evaluate them in the situations where people actually use them, because doing well on a benchmark is only part of the story.

I also don’t think trust should be all or nothing. You might trust an AI to help you brainstorm, but require much stronger verification before letting it make a medical decision. The level of autonomy should match the consequences of a mistake.

So rather than starting by treating AI as a trustworthy entity, I would start by building systems whose behavior we can examine, correct, and hold accountable through the people and institutions deploying them. Trust should grow as we demonstrate reliability, not simply as the system becomes more fluent or more humanlike.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what makes AI trustworthy but does not ask why people trust children or other people while fearing AI.

r002.rationale: The response calls for examining and evaluating AI behavior, but does not identify improving trustworthiness as a reason to develop world models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish intelligence from trustworthiness. A system can be very capable and still make mistakes, misunderstand your intent, or give a confident answer when it doesn’t know. So greater intelligence doesn’t automatically solve the trust problem.

For me, trust has to be earned through behavior. Can we evaluate the system in the situations where people will actually use it? Can it communicate uncertainty, accept corrections, and let a human intervene? We need to understand where it fails, not just show where it succeeds.

And the standard depends on the application. If an AI helps you brainstorm, a mistake may be harmless. If it makes a medical recommendation or controls a robot, the consequences are very different. You need much stronger evidence and safeguards.

So I would approach this as an ongoing engineering and social process. Build useful systems, study their failures, make responsibility clear, and expand their autonomy as the evidence supports it. The goal shouldn’t be to persuade people to trust AI. It should be to make that trust justified.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how AI can earn trust but does not ask why people trust children and other people while fearing AI.

r002.rationale: It does not mention world models or identify improving trustworthiness as a reason to develop them.
